claim: Freezing of gait (FoG) in Parkinson's disease (PD) is an incapacitating transient phenomenon, followed by continuous postural disorders.
source: Freezing of gait (FoG) in Parkinson's disease (PD) is an incapacitating transient phenomenon, followed by continuous postural disorders.
evidence: This is a general characterization statement about FoG in PD, drawing from established clinical knowledge.

claim: Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is a promising intervention for FoG in patients with PD.
source: Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is a promising intervention for FoG in patients with PD, however, its effects on distinct domains of postural control is not well known.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of research and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The effects of SCS on distinct domains of postural control is not well known.
source: Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is a promising intervention for FoG in patients with PD, however, its effects on distinct domains of postural control is not well known.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the literature.

claim: Four patients with FoG were implanted with SCS systems in the upper thoracic spine.
source: Four patients with FoG were implanted with SCS systems in the upper thoracic spine.
evidence: This describes the study design and patient population.

claim: SCS improved FoG and APA in general.
source: In general, the results showed that SCS improved FoG and APA.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's main findings based on experimental data.

claim: SCS failed to improve reactive postural responses.
source: However, SCS failed to improve reactive postural responses.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the experimental data.

claim: SCS seems to influence cortical motor circuits, involving the supplementary motor area.
source: SCS seems to influence cortical motor circuits, involving the supplementary motor area.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the study findings and existing knowledge.

claim: Reactive posture control to external perturbation mainly relies on neuronal circuitries involving the brainstem and spinal cord.
source: On the other hand, reactive posture control to external perturbation that mainly relies on neuronal circuitries involving the brainstem and spinal cord, is less influenced by SCS.
evidence: This draws from established neurophysiological knowledge.

claim: Reactive posture control is less influenced by SCS.
source: On the other hand, reactive posture control to external perturbation that mainly relies on neuronal circuitries involving the brainstem and spinal cord, is less influenced by SCS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Postural instability and gait disorders (PIGD) are debilitating phenomena that frequently impair locomotion and can significantly affect the quality of life in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients.
source: Postural instability and gait disorders (PIGD) are debilitating phenomena that frequently impair locomotion and can significantly affect the quality of life in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients (Perez-Lloret et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PIGD is the most common cause of falls, which are associated with increase in morbimortality in PD.
source: PIGD is the most common cause of falls, which are associated with increase in morbimortality in PD (Bloem et al., 2004; Delval et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Freezing of gait (FoG) is described as brief and episodic absence or marked reduction of the anterior progression of the feet, despite the intention to walk.
source: Freezing of gait (FoG) is described as brief and episodic absence or marked reduction of the anterior progression of the feet, despite the intention to walk (Giladi and Nieuwboer, 2008).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: Normal gait requires an exact coordination of postural adjustment in advance of each step forward, namely anticipatory postural adjustment (APA).
source: Normal gait requires an exact coordination of postural adjustment in advance of each step forward, namely anticipatory postural adjustment (APA) (de Lima-Pardini et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: During imminent FoG episodes, the intention to walk is uncoupled from the triggering of APA, with consequent failure of the forward movement.
source: During imminent FoG episodes, the intention to walk is uncoupled from the triggering of APA, with consequent failure of the forward movement.
evidence: This describes a mechanism based on established knowledge.

claim: In PD, FoG episodes are associated with deficient APA.
source: In PD, FoG episodes are associated with deficient APA (Mancini et al., 2016; Schlenstedt et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: FoG is mainly associated with disorders of frontal cortical regions (e.g. supplementary motor area - SMA) that comprise a known brain circuitry dedicated to APA control.
source: Physiological evidence, functional imaging and clinical-pathological studies suggest that FoG is mainly associated with disorders of frontal cortical regions (e.g. supplementary motor area - SMA) that comprise a known brain circuitry dedicated to APA control (de Lima-Pardini et al., 2017; Jacobs et al., 2009a; Bolzoni et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The occurrence of FoG is highly influenced by attention, environmental triggers and dopaminergic drugs.
source: The occurrence of FoG is highly influenced by attention, environmental triggers and dopaminergic drugs, suggesting the existence of complex mechanisms involving brainstem locomotor networks, the basal ganglia and cortical regions (Jacobs et al., 2009a; Deecke, 1987; Coelho and Teixeira, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: FoG involves complex mechanisms involving brainstem locomotor networks, the basal ganglia and cortical regions.
source: The occurrence of FoG is highly influenced by attention, environmental triggers and dopaminergic drugs, suggesting the existence of complex mechanisms involving brainstem locomotor networks, the basal ganglia and cortical regions (Jacobs et al., 2009a; Deecke, 1987; Coelho and Teixeira, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: Automatic balance control seems to be mediated mainly by brainstem circuits, being less sensitive to attentional and environmental disturbances.
source: On the other hand, automatic balance control seems to be mediated mainly by brainstem circuits, being less sensitive to attentional and environmental disturbances (Horak and Diener, 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: SCS could enhance locomotion in PD models in mice.
source: Since the first experimental report from Fuentes et al. (Fuentes et al., 2009) showing that SCS could enhance locomotion in PD models in mice, and more recently in primates by possibly shifting the brain pathological oscillatory activity (Santana et al., 2014), SCS began to figure as a possible treatment for FoG in PD.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fuentes et al., 2009.

claim: SCS in primates possibly shifts the brain pathological oscillatory activity.
source: Since the first experimental report from Fuentes et al. (Fuentes et al., 2009) showing that SCS could enhance locomotion in PD models in mice, and more recently in primates by possibly shifting the brain pathological oscillatory activity (Santana et al., 2014), SCS began to figure as a possible treatment for FoG in PD.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Santana et al., 2014.

claim: Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) improves treatment-resistant postural and gait disorders in patients with PD.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that spinal cord stimulation (SCS) improves treatment-resistant postural and gait disorders in patients with PD (de Andrade et al., 2016; Nishioka and Nakajima, 2015; Yadav and Nicolelis, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In primates, SCS increases neuronal firing of the primary motor cortex.
source: In primates, SCS increases neuronal firing of the primary motor cortex, and decreases pathological cortico-striatal synchronous low-frequency waves showing that SCS does influence the oscillatory activity in brain motor circuits (Fuentes et al., 2009; Bentley et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In primates, SCS decreases pathological cortico-striatal synchronous low-frequency waves.
source: In primates, SCS increases neuronal firing of the primary motor cortex, and decreases pathological cortico-striatal synchronous low-frequency waves showing that SCS does influence the oscillatory activity in brain motor circuits (Fuentes et al., 2009; Bentley et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: SCS influences the oscillatory activity in brain motor circuits.
source: In primates, SCS increases neuronal firing of the primary motor cortex, and decreases pathological cortico-striatal synchronous low-frequency waves showing that SCS does influence the oscillatory activity in brain motor circuits (Fuentes et al., 2009; Bentley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: SCS may disrupt the aberrant inhibition of the globus pallidus internus onto thalamus and SMA.
source: In fact, SCS may disrupt the aberrant inhibition of the globus pallidus internus onto thalamus and SMA (Brudzynski et al., 1993; Takakusaki, 2017).
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation supported by citations.

claim: The SMA has cortifugal projections to pedunculopontine nuclei (PPN).
source: As part of the circuit that controls APA, the SMA has cortifugal projections to pedunculopontine nuclei (PPN), a region particularly involved in gait initiation (Takakusaki, 2017; Aravamuthan et al., 2009).
evidence: This anatomical statement is supported by citations.

claim: PPN is a region particularly involved in gait initiation.
source: As part of the circuit that controls APA, the SMA has cortifugal projections to pedunculopontine nuclei (PPN), a region particularly involved in gait initiation (Takakusaki, 2017; Aravamuthan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The activity of SMA, globus pallidus and PPN are impaired in patients with FoG.
source: Since the activity of SMA, globus pallidus and PPN are impaired in patients with FoG (Snijders et al., 2016), SCS would be able to modulate this circuit and improve APA and gait initiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: SCS would be able to modulate the circuit involving SMA, globus pallidus and PPN and improve APA and gait initiation.
source: Since the activity of SMA, globus pallidus and PPN are impaired in patients with FoG (Snijders et al., 2016), SCS would be able to modulate this circuit and improve APA and gait initiation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from cited evidence.

claim: High-frequency SCS (300 Hz) improved gait performance in various gait tests.
source: Recently, our group reported positive effects of high-frequency SCS (300 Hz) on gait, improving the performance in various gait tests, which were reproduced during double-blinded assessments.
evidence: This refers to previous findings from the research group.

claim: Continuous SCS chronically reduced FoG episodes.
source: Also, continuous SCS chronically reduced FoG episodes, improved unified Parkinson's disease rating scale (UPDRS)-III motor scale scores and of self-reported quality of life (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Continuous SCS improved unified Parkinson's disease rating scale (UPDRS)-III motor scale scores.
source: Also, continuous SCS chronically reduced FoG episodes, improved unified Parkinson's disease rating scale (UPDRS)-III motor scale scores and of self-reported quality of life (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Continuous SCS improved self-reported quality of life.
source: Also, continuous SCS chronically reduced FoG episodes, improved unified Parkinson's disease rating scale (UPDRS)-III motor scale scores and of self-reported quality of life (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: SCS at higher density stimulation parameters (200–500 μs/30–130 Hz) improved gait and FoG in PD patients.
source: However, recent studies have shown that SCS at higher density stimulation parameters (200–500 μs/30–130 Hz) also improved gait and FoG in PD patients (Samotus et al., 2018) or at 70–100 Hz in primary freezing of gait when applied at T8-T10 spinal segments (Rohani et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: SCS at 70–100 Hz improved primary freezing of gait when applied at T8-T10 spinal segments.
source: However, recent studies have shown that SCS at higher density stimulation parameters (200–500 μs/30–130 Hz) also improved gait and FoG in PD patients (Samotus et al., 2018) or at 70–100 Hz in primary freezing of gait when applied at T8-T10 spinal segments (Rohani et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: During 300 Hz-SCS, all participants showed significant decrease of APA duration compared to OFF.
source: During 300 Hz-SCS, all participants showed significant decrease of APA duration compared to OFF (Figure 1C) (p=0.042).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: For the 60 Hz-SCS, participants 1 and 2 showed shortened APA duration.
source: For the 60 Hz-SCS, while participants 1 and 2 showed shortened APA duration, participants 3 and 4 showed increased APA duration as compared to the OFF condition, failing to show significance (p=0.866).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data.

claim: For the 60 Hz-SCS, participants 3 and 4 showed increased APA duration as compared to the OFF condition.
source: For the 60 Hz-SCS, while participants 1 and 2 showed shortened APA duration, participants 3 and 4 showed increased APA duration as compared to the OFF condition, failing to show significance (p=0.866).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data.

claim: 60 Hz-SCS failed to show significant change in APA duration compared to OFF condition.
source: For the 60 Hz-SCS, while participants 1 and 2 showed shortened APA duration, participants 3 and 4 showed increased APA duration as compared to the OFF condition, failing to show significance (p=0.866).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data.

claim: All participants showed increased amplitude (peak) of APA, except for participant 4 at 60 Hz.
source: Descriptive values of amplitude (peak) of APA showed increased values in all participants, except for the participant 4 at 60 Hz (Figure 1A), without reaching significance compared to OFF condition (p=0.177).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The amplitude of APA did not reach significance compared to OFF condition.
source: Descriptive values of amplitude (peak) of APA showed increased values in all participants, except for the participant 4 at 60 Hz (Figure 1A), without reaching significance compared to OFF condition (p=0.177).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data.

claim: Patients 2 and 3 showed significant reduction of FoG duration during 300 Hz SCS only.
source: The improvement in FoG observed in a preliminary report (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017) was reproduced in this trial with patients 2 and 3 showing significant reduction of FoG duration during 300 Hz SCS only (p=0.042).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Patients 1 and 4 did not experience any FoG episodes during the biomechanical assessment in the Gait Laboratory in any condition.
source: Patients 1 and 4 did not experience any FoG episodes during the biomechanical assessment in the Gait Laboratory in any condition (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The results of SCS over the amplitude of COMap and COPap did not show significant changes for 60 Hz when compared to OFF state.
source: Considering the reactive postural control, the results of SCS over the amplitude of COMap and COPap did not show significant changes for 60 (p=0.860) and 300 Hz (p=0.220) when compared to OFF state.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The results of SCS over the amplitude of COMap and COPap did not show significant changes for 300 Hz when compared to OFF state.
source: Considering the reactive postural control, the results of SCS over the amplitude of COMap and COPap did not show significant changes for 60 (p=0.860) and 300 Hz (p=0.220) when compared to OFF state.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: Subject two had higher COMap (worse performance) during both 60 Hz and 300 Hz SCS compared to OFF state.
source: Note that subject two had higher COMap (worse performance) during both 60 Hz and 300 Hz SCS, and higher COP (worse performance) during 60 Hz SCS compared to OFF state.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Subject two had higher COP (worse performance) during 60 Hz SCS compared to OFF state.
source: Note that subject two had higher COMap (worse performance) during both 60 Hz and 300 Hz SCS, and higher COP (worse performance) during 60 Hz SCS compared to OFF state.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Normal gait requires adequate coordination between the APA and limb movements.
source: While normal gait requires adequate coordination between the APA and limb movements (de Lima-Pardini et al., 2017), FoG episodes are thought to involve defective APA resulting in difficulty or cessation of gait initiation (Schlenstedt et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2009b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: FoG episodes are thought to involve defective APA resulting in difficulty or cessation of gait initiation.
source: While normal gait requires adequate coordination between the APA and limb movements (de Lima-Pardini et al., 2017), FoG episodes are thought to involve defective APA resulting in difficulty or cessation of gait initiation (Schlenstedt et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2009b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: SCS at 300 Hz was effective in reducing the duration of APA.
source: In the present study, data showed that SCS at 300 Hz was effective in reducing the duration of APA and reducing the time of FoG.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings based on experimental data.

claim: SCS at 300 Hz was effective in reducing the time of FoG.
source: In the present study, data showed that SCS at 300 Hz was effective in reducing the duration of APA and reducing the time of FoG.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings based on experimental data.

claim: SCS at 60 Hz failed to improve gait and APA.
source: Conversely, we observed that SCS at 60 Hz failed to improve gait and APA.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant improvement in FoG when 60 Hz-SCS was applied.
source: Corroborating clinical results, there was no significant improvement in FoG in the present study, neither in our preliminary report when 60 Hz-SCS was applied (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data and previous work.

claim: Two patients did not experience any FoG episodes during laboratory examination, even when SCS was OFF for a period longer than their carry-over effect lasted.
source: Unexpectedly, two patients did not experience any FoG episodes during laboratory examination, even when SCS was OFF for a period longer than their carry-over effect lasted.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: FoG is an episodic phenomenon, and even severe patients may not exhibit FoG in the laboratory.
source: Being the FoG an episodic phenomenon, even severe patients may not exhibit FoG in the laboratory (Nutt et al., 2011; Giladi et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The time of FoG was reduced in 2 subjects during 300 Hz SCS.
source: Conversely, the time of FoG was reduced in the other 2 subjects during 300 Hz SCS.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: All subjects experienced frequent FoG episodes and were responsive to 300 Hz SCS in the outpatient clinic.
source: In the previous report, we showed that all subjects did experience frequent FoG episodes and were responsive to 300 Hz SCS in the outpatient clinic (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017).
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous report.

claim: SCS at 300 Hz is more effective than SCS at 60 Hz in improving FoG and correcting APAs.
source: Nonetheless, our findings suggest that SCS at 300 Hz is more effective than SCS at 60 Hz (both with pulse width at 90 μs and amplitudes at 105% of sensory threshold) in improving FoG and correcting APAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Circuits involving the supplementary motor area (SMA) are thought to modulate APA.
source: Circuits involving the supplementary motor area (SMA) are thought to modulate APA (Takakusaki, 2017), specifically in its timing (Jacobs et al., 2009a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: SMA specifically modulates the timing of APA.
source: Circuits involving the supplementary motor area (SMA) are thought to modulate APA (Takakusaki, 2017), specifically in its timing (Jacobs et al., 2009a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Timing, but not amplitude of APA was improved by SCS at 300 Hz.
source: Our results showed that timing, but not amplitude of APA was improved by SCS at 300 Hz, which could indicate that motor circuits involving SMA were also influenced.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The improvement in timing but not amplitude of APA could indicate that motor circuits involving SMA were influenced by SCS.
source: Our results showed that timing, but not amplitude of APA was improved by SCS at 300 Hz, which could indicate that motor circuits involving SMA were also influenced.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: SCS modulates cortical function of primary sensory and motor areas, in addition to the prefrontal, cingulate and insula cortices, and thalamus in humans and animals.
source: Although data showing that SCS directly modulates SMA still lacks, extensive data show that SCS modulates cortical function of primary sensory and motor areas, in addition to the prefrontal, cingulate and insula cortices, and thalamus in humans and animals (Fuentes et al., 2009; Santana et al., 2014; Bentley et al., 2016; Stancák et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Inputs from ascending leminiscal and extralemniscal pathways to the brainstem and thalamus may modulate SMA.
source: Inputs from ascending leminiscal and extralemniscal pathways to the brainstem and thalamus that may modulate SMA are also highly connected to the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN), a locomotor region in the brainstem involved in the control of movement initiation and body equilibrium (Takakusaki, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Ascending pathways to the brainstem and thalamus are highly connected to the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN).
source: Inputs from ascending leminiscal and extralemniscal pathways to the brainstem and thalamus that may modulate SMA are also highly connected to the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN), a locomotor region in the brainstem involved in the control of movement initiation and body equilibrium (Takakusaki, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: PPN is a locomotor region in the brainstem involved in the control of movement initiation and body equilibrium.
source: Inputs from ascending leminiscal and extralemniscal pathways to the brainstem and thalamus that may modulate SMA are also highly connected to the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN), a locomotor region in the brainstem involved in the control of movement initiation and body equilibrium (Takakusaki, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Ascending stimulation of the thalamic-cortical-striatum loop delivered by SCS may disrupt the aberrant inhibition of the globus pallidus internus onto thalamus and PPN.
source: It is thought that ascending stimulation of the thalamic-cortical-striatum loop delivered by SCS may disrupt the aberrant inhibition of the globus pallidus internus onto thalamus and PPN, facilitating the reticulospinal tract and, consequently, activating central pattern generators (CPG) in the spinal cord (Brudzynski et al., 1993; Takakusaki, 2017).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: SCS facilitates the reticulospinal tract.
source: It is thought that ascending stimulation of the thalamic-cortical-striatum loop delivered by SCS may disrupt the aberrant inhibition of the globus pallidus internus onto thalamus and PPN, facilitating the reticulospinal tract and, consequently, activating central pattern generators (CPG) in the spinal cord (Brudzynski et al., 1993; Takakusaki, 2017).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: SCS activates central pattern generators (CPG) in the spinal cord.
source: It is thought that ascending stimulation of the thalamic-cortical-striatum loop delivered by SCS may disrupt the aberrant inhibition of the globus pallidus internus onto thalamus and PPN, facilitating the reticulospinal tract and, consequently, activating central pattern generators (CPG) in the spinal cord (Brudzynski et al., 1993; Takakusaki, 2017).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Facilitation of the thalamic-cortical-striatum loop occurs due to the inhibition of abnormal synchronous beta frequency neuronal oscillations.
source: According to previous studies in animals, facilitation of the thalamic-cortical-striatum loop occurs due to the inhibition of abnormal synchronous beta frequency neuronal oscillations (Fuentes et al., 2009; Santana et al., 2014; Yadav and Nicolelis, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: The reactive posture control was not affected by SCS in both conditions.
source: We also observed that the reactive posture control was not affected by SCS in both conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: One participant showed poorer reactive postural control in both stimulation frequencies, but still exhibited positive response in APA and FoG.
source: In fact, one of the participants showed poorer reactive postural control in both stimulation frequencies, but still exhibiting positive response in APA and FoG.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: A case study found improvements in gait with no changes in reactive postural control after SCS.
source: While a case study also found improvements in gait with no changes in reactive postural control after SCS (Landi et al., 2013), another report showed an effect of SCS in reactive postural responses (Agari and Date, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Another report showed an effect of SCS in reactive postural responses.
source: While a case study also found improvements in gait with no changes in reactive postural control after SCS (Landi et al., 2013), another report showed an effect of SCS in reactive postural responses (Agari and Date, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Previous studies assessed responses to perturbation by the pull test, which is a qualitative measurement influenced by a subjective impression of the evaluator.
source: These studies, however, assessed responses to perturbation by the pull test, which is a qualitative measurement influenced by a subjective impression of the evaluator.
evidence: This is a critique of previous methodologies.

claim: The present study employed a systematic method to quantify FoG, considered more reliable than the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire alone.
source: It is worth noting that we employed a systematic method to quantify FoG, considered more reliable than the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire (Giladi et al., 2000) alone.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: SCS apparently improves FoG and APA and does not influence reactive posture control.
source: Based on the present data and in our previous results, SCS apparently improves FoG and APA and does not influence reactive posture control.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: SCS might differently affect reactive and anticipatory mechanisms of postural control.
source: It is possible that SCS might differently affect these two mechanisms of postural control – reactive and anticipatory.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: APA mechanisms are dependent of thalamo-cortical-striatum loops highly influenced by attentional and environmental changes.
source: APA mechanisms are dependent of thalamo-cortical-striatum loops highly influenced by attentional and environmental changes (Takakusaki, 2017; Jacobs and Horak, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Reactive posture control to external and unpredictable triggers relies on neuronal circuitries involving the brainstem and spinal cord with less cortical influence from the cortex.
source: On the other hand, unlike APAs, reactive posture control to external and unpredictable triggers relies on neuronal circuitries involving the brainstem and spinal cord with less cortical influence from the cortex (Jacobs and Horak, 2007; Honeycutt et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Circuits that depend on cortical influence are more sensitive to SCS.
source: It is possible that circuits that depend on cortical influence are more sensitive to SCS, given the increasing in cortical input to the striatum that reaches structures involved in planning of movement, required during APAs but not during unpredictable external perturbations (Krishnamurthi et al., 2012; Bleuse et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations.

claim: SCS increases cortical input to the striatum that reaches structures involved in planning of movement.
source: It is possible that circuits that depend on cortical influence are more sensitive to SCS, given the increasing in cortical input to the striatum that reaches structures involved in planning of movement, required during APAs but not during unpredictable external perturbations (Krishnamurthi et al., 2012; Bleuse et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations.

claim: Movement planning is required during APAs but not during unpredictable external perturbations.
source: It is possible that circuits that depend on cortical influence are more sensitive to SCS, given the increasing in cortical input to the striatum that reaches structures involved in planning of movement, required during APAs but not during unpredictable external perturbations (Krishnamurthi et al., 2012; Bleuse et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about motor control mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: SCS did not improve reactive postural control, similar to what has been found for DBS.
source: Similarly to what have been found for DBS, our results suggest that SCS did not improve reactive postural control (St George et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison of findings supported by a citation.

claim: DBS initially improves FoG and gait.
source: Although there is evidence that DBS initially improves FoG and gait (Schlenstedt et al., 2017), biomechanical and laboratory findings on APA are still conflicting.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Biomechanical and laboratory findings on APA for DBS are still conflicting.
source: Although there is evidence that DBS initially improves FoG and gait (Schlenstedt et al., 2017), biomechanical and laboratory findings on APA are still conflicting.
evidence: This characterizes the state of the literature.

claim: DBS impairs APA during step initiation.
source: A few studies show that DBS impairs APA during step initiation (Muniz et al., 2010) even when administered in the ON levodopa state (Rocchi et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: DBS impairs APA even when administered in the ON levodopa state.
source: A few studies show that DBS impairs APA during step initiation (Muniz et al., 2010) even when administered in the ON levodopa state (Rocchi et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Continuous stimulation of circuits in the subthalamic region may lead to plastic changes that impaired step initiation.
source: These results suggest that continuous stimulation of circuits in the subthalamic region may lead to plastic changes that impaired step initiation.
evidence: This is an inference from cited studies.

claim: DBS corrects cardinal symptoms of PD and dyskinesias.
source: While DBS corrects cardinal symptoms of PD and dyskinesias, it does not seem to substantially affect APA and FoG.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about DBS.

claim: DBS does not seem to substantially affect APA and FoG.
source: While DBS corrects cardinal symptoms of PD and dyskinesias, it does not seem to substantially affect APA and FoG.
evidence: This is an inference from the literature and study findings.

claim: SCS can improve FoG and APA in both DBS ON and OFF medication conditions.
source: In contrast, SCS can improve FoG and APA in both DBS ON and OFF medication conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: SCS and DBS could be mechanistically and clinically complementary.
source: These collective results suggest that SCS and DBS could be mechanistically and clinically complementary.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the comparison of findings.

claim: The effects of SCS observed clinically in FOG are followed by an improvement in APA during step initiation.
source: In conclusion, our findings suggest that the effects of SCS observed clinically in FOG are followed by an improvement in APA during step initiation, but not by changes in reactive postural control.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The effects of SCS observed clinically in FOG are not followed by changes in reactive postural control.
source: In conclusion, our findings suggest that the effects of SCS observed clinically in FOG are followed by an improvement in APA during step initiation, but not by changes in reactive postural control.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

source: Patients included in the present study participated in the clinical trial also registered in the clinicaltrials.gov (#NCT02388204).

source: All experiments were performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2002).

claim: Four patients with PIGD previously treated with bilateral STN DBS were implanted with SCS systems in the upper thoracic spine (T2-T4).
source: Four patients with PIGD previously treated with bilateral STN DBS were implanted with SCS systems in the upper thoracic spine (T2-T4) (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the study population and intervention.

claim: Patients were tested for the effects of SCS on APA, and postural reactive responses related to postural and balance control.
source: Patients were tested for the effects of SCS on APA, and postural reactive responses related to postural and balance control.
evidence: This describes the study assessments.

claim: Assessments were performed in OFF SCS, ON SCS at 60 Hz, and ON SCS at 300 Hz conditions.
source: Assessments were performed in the following conditions: (Perez-Lloret et al., 2014) OFF SCS; (Bloem et al., 2004) ON SCS at 60 Hz; and (Delval et al., 2014) ON SCS at 300 Hz with or without medication (ON/OFF meds) for at least 12 hr.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Conditions were randomized and tested at least one week apart.
source: These conditions were randomized and tested at least one week apart.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: 60 Hz SCS and 300 Hz SCS generated undistinguished paresthesias.
source: 60 Hz SCS and 300 Hz were applied as active condition since they generated undistinguished paresthesias, but in average 60 Hz exerted no significant effects in gait, while 300 Hz elicited substantial improvement (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the stimulation parameters used.

claim: 60 Hz SCS exerted no significant effects in gait on average.
source: 60 Hz SCS and 300 Hz were applied as active condition since they generated undistinguished paresthesias, but in average 60 Hz exerted no significant effects in gait, while 300 Hz elicited substantial improvement (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work.

claim: 300 Hz SCS elicited substantial improvement in gait.
source: 60 Hz SCS and 300 Hz were applied as active condition since they generated undistinguished paresthesias, but in average 60 Hz exerted no significant effects in gait, while 300 Hz elicited substantial improvement (Pinto de Souza et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work.

claim: FoG was assessed using a wireless accelerometer placed on the lumbar region during a 10 m walk task.
source: FoG was assessed using a wireless accelerometer (Delsys, Trigno Delsys Inc., USA; filter: Butterworth, low-pass at 10 Hz) placed on the lumbar region during a 10 m walk task.
evidence: This describes the methodology for FoG assessment.

claim: Three 10 m walking trials were performed.
source: Three 10 m walking trials were performed.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Patients were assessed during step initiation with the less affected leg, having both feet positioned on a force platform.
source: To quantify APA, the patients were next assessed during step initiation with the less affected leg, having both feet positioned on a force platform (AMTI, OR6-6, Advanced Mechanical Technology Inc., USA; with an internal analog low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency set at 100 Hz).
evidence: This describes the methodology for APA assessment.

claim: A reflective marker on the less affected leg was used to identify the onset of the step through a motion analysis system.
source: A reflective marker on the less affected leg (defined from the UPDRS part III) was used to identify the onset of the step through a motion analysis system (Vicon Nexus V.1.8, UK, with four cameras T10 - RRID:SCR_015001).
evidence: This describes the methodology for step detection.

claim: The APA forces of the more affected side (contralateral limb to the stepping leg) were considered for the analysis.
source: The APA forces of the more affected side (contralateral limb to the stepping leg) were considered for the analysis.
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach.

claim: Participants performed a single block of 10 trials of step initiation, with intertrial intervals of approximately 30 s.
source: Participants performed a single block of 10 trials of step initiation, with intertrial intervals of approximately 30 s.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Participants used no physical support or sensory cueing to perform the step.
source: They used no physical support or sensory cueing to perform the step.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Reactive postural control was assessed using a custom-built movable force platform with an integrated force plate as the base of support.
source: Reactive postural control was assessed using a custom-built movable force platform with an integrated force plate as the base of support (Coelho and Teixeira, 2017).
evidence: This describes the methodology for reactive postural control assessment.

claim: The task consisted of recovering stable body equilibrium following unanticipated backward displacement of the supporting platform, while maintaining the feet in place.
source: The task consisted of recovering stable body equilibrium following unanticipated backward displacement of the supporting platform, while maintaining the feet in place.
evidence: This describes the experimental task.

claim: Platform perturbations used amplitude of 12 cm, peak velocity of 15 cm/s, and peak acceleration of 100 cm/s2.
source: The following parameters for platform perturbations were used: amplitude of 12 cm, peak velocity of 15 cm/s, and peak acceleration of 100 cm/s2.
evidence: This describes the perturbation parameters.

claim: Perturbations were preceded by randomly varied preparatory intervals, ranging 1–3 s, to prevent anticipation.
source: Perturbations were preceded by randomly varied preparatory intervals, ranging 1–3 s, to prevent anticipation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design to prevent anticipation.

claim: The duration of FoG was calculated in the frequency domain based on the method proposed by Moore et al.
source: The duration of FoG was calculated in the frequency domain based on the method proposed by Moore et al. (Moore et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2008), in which the frequency band of the acceleration during normal gait (0–3 Hz) and freezing (3–8 Hz) may be distinguished during walking through changes in frequency power (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The frequency band of the acceleration during normal gait is 0–3 Hz.
source: The duration of FoG was calculated in the frequency domain based on the method proposed by Moore et al. (Moore et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2008), in which the frequency band of the acceleration during normal gait (0–3 Hz) and freezing (3–8 Hz) may be distinguished during walking through changes in frequency power (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is a methodological detail based on cited work.

claim: The frequency band of the acceleration during freezing is 3–8 Hz.
source: The duration of FoG was calculated in the frequency domain based on the method proposed by Moore et al. (Moore et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2008), in which the frequency band of the acceleration during normal gait (0–3 Hz) and freezing (3–8 Hz) may be distinguished during walking through changes in frequency power (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is a methodological detail based on cited work.

claim: Sampling windows of 7.5 s of the lumbar acceleration were defined for the spectrum analysis.
source: Sampling windows of 7.5 s of the lumbar acceleration were defined for the spectrum analysis.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: The index of FoG is calculated by dividing the peak power of the FoG band (3–8 Hz) by the peak power of the normal gait (0.5–3 Hz).
source: In each sampling window, the peak power was calculated for the FoG band (3–8 Hz) and divided by the peak power of the normal gait (0.5–3 Hz). This metric is referred to as the index of FoG.
evidence: This describes the calculation method for the FoG index.

claim: Values above the clinical threshold of 2 for the FoG index were considered as FoG events.
source: Values above the clinical threshold of 2 were considerate as FoG events (Moore et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the threshold for identifying FoG events based on cited work.

claim: Onset of the APA was defined as the time between the abrupt increase of the mediolateral displacement and the onset of the step.
source: For analysis of the stepping task, onset of the APA was defined as the time between the abrupt increase of the mediolateral displacement, defined as two standard deviations above the mean of the baseline force, and the onset of the step, defined as two standard deviations above the mean of the baseline foot displacement in the anteroposterior direction (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The time of APA was calculated as the time between the onset of APA and the onset of the step.
source: Based on these measurements, the time of APA was calculated as the time between the onset of APA and the onset of the step.
evidence: This describes the calculation method.

claim: Mediolateral force amplitude during the step task was normalized by the individual foot size (unit in N/cm).
source: Mediolateral force amplitude during the step task was normalized by the individual foot size (unit in N/cm).
evidence: This describes the normalization method.

claim: Root mean square of anteroposterior displacement of the center of mass (COMap) and center of pressure (COPap) were assessed for reactive postural control.
source: For analysis of reactive postural control during perturbation trials, root mean square of anteroposterior displacement of the center of mass (COMap) and center of pressure (COPap) were assessed.
evidence: This describes the outcome measures for reactive postural control.

claim: Spherical reflective markers were attached at specific anatomical points on the right hemibody to calculate COMap.
source: To calculate COMap, spherical reflective markers were attached at the following anatomical points on the right hemibody: ﬁfth metatarsophalangeal joint, lateral malleolus, lateral knee joint center, greater trochanter and the approximate axis of shoulder rotation (Figure 2DE).
evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating COMap with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Data sampling frequency was set at 200 Hz for kinematics and ground reaction forces.
source: Data sampling frequency was set at 200 Hz for kinematics and ground reaction forces.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: Kinematic and ground reaction force data were digitally low-pass filtered with a cut-off frequency of 10 Hz.
source: Kinematic and ground reaction force data were digitally low-pass filtered with a cut-off frequency of 10 Hz.
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: Signals were filtered through a dual-pass fourth-order Butterworth filter.
source: Signals were filtered through a dual-pass fourth-order Butterworth filter.
evidence: This describes the filtering method.

claim: Estimation of CoMap displacement was based on the anthropometric model proposed by Winter.
source: Estimation of CoMap displacement was based on the anthropometric model proposed by Winter (Winter, 1991), assuming symmetric displacement between two body sides.
evidence: This describes the calculation method based on a cited model.

claim: Analysis was performed on trial averages of each subject and each stimulation condition for the four subjects.
source: Analysis was performed on trial averages of each subject and each stimulation condition (OFF, 60 Hz, 300 Hz) for the four subjects.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis approach.

claim: The percentage of change in the ON vs. OFF stimulation conditions was calculated using the formula: %Change = (ON (60 or 300 Hz)-OFF)/OFF.
source: We then calculated the percentage of change in the ON (60 Hz and 300 Hz) vs. OFF stimulation conditions using the following calculation: %Change = (ON (60 or 300 Hz)-OFF)/OFF.
evidence: This describes the calculation method for percent change.

claim: Improvement was referred as positive values of % change.
source: Improvement was referred as positive values of % change (decrease in gait time, shortening of FoG time, increasing of the amplitude of APA and decreasing of APA duration).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the percent change values.

claim: Negative values of % change were considered as performance decline.
source: Negative values were considered as performance decline.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the percent change values.

claim: Group averages of percent change for each variable were compared to the basal condition (OFF, no gain) using Student's t test.
source: Group averages of percent change for each variable were compared to the basal condition (OFF, no gain) using Student's t test.
evidence: This describes the statistical test used.

claim: p-value was set at ≤0.05 for each ON condition (60 and 300 Hz).
source: p-value set at ≤0.05 for each ON condition (60 and 300 Hz).
evidence: This describes the statistical significance threshold.
